g.text: Repair time is a durability parameter, not an operations metric
The naive calculation understates real durability by four orders of magnitude, because it assumes no repair ever happens.
EC 8+4: any 8 of 12 fragments reconstruct the object
so no DC holds only parity.
Parity is as good as data:
Lose any 4 fragments -> reconstruct. Lose one entire DC (4 fragments) -> SURVIVES, with EXACTLY ZERO MARGIN.
Lose one DC plus any single further drive -> DATA LOSS.
"Survives the loss of a datacentre" and "survives it with headroom" are different promises, and this layout only makes the first.
That is why repair becomes the highest-priority workload in the cluster the moment a DC drops.
The model almost everyone gets wrong
assumes a dead drive is NEVER replaced
This asks: what is the chance all three drives
die at some point this year? Only the right
question if nothing is ever repaired.
Data is lost only if the REMAINING copies fail
inside the repair window. Each extra copy adds
another factor of lambda*T - and lambda*T is tiny.
6 hours to 7 days costs THREE FULL NINES. T is
squared for replication and raised to the 4th for
8+4 - so halving repair time is worth 4x to 16x.
Repair bandwidth is a durability budget line.
The catch that stops EC winning everywhere
Rebuilding one lost 10 MB fragment means READING
8 fragments - 80 MB. So EC repair costs 8x the
bandwidth, which lengthens MTTR, which REDUCES
durability. The two effects fight each other.
So: 3x replication under 1 MB (8 seeks to read 500 KB is unaffordable against a 150-IOPS budget), EC 8+4 above it.
Small objects are 20% of the COUNT but under 1% of the BYTES - so replicating them costs a rounding error of capacity.
